name: Authentication & Passwords
description: Password security, biometrics, multi-factor and passwordless authentication (FIDO/WebAuthn).

ccs.narrative:
Authentication research at CCS has covered the full lifecycle of credential security, from password strength estimation to biometric modalities and passwordless standards. On the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters (CCS 2018) revealed that deployed meters systematically misestimate real-world password strength, undermining user guidance at scale. A Formal Analysis of 5G Authentication (CCS 2018) contributed on the protocol side, formally verifying the 5G AKA handshake. CAPTCHA-breaking received renewed attention with Yet Another Text Captcha Solver: A Generative Adversarial Network Based Approach (CCS 2018), which demonstrated GAN-based solvers require only small training sets.

Compromised credential management became practical in 2019: Protocols for Checking Compromised Credentials (CCS 2019) designed privacy-preserving protocols enabling users to check breached credentials without exposing them to the checking service. Domain Validation++ For MitM-Resilient PKI (CCS 2018) strengthened certificate issuance against network-level adversaries.

Beyond passwords, sensor-based authentication expanded. PatternListener: Cracking Android Pattern Lock Using Acoustic Signals (CCS 2018) cracked gesture-based locks acoustically, DeMiCPU: Device Fingerprinting with Magnetic Signals Radiated by CPU (CCS 2019) fingerprinted hardware using magnetic emissions, and EchoHand: High Accuracy and Presentation Attack Resistant Hand Authentication on Commodity Mobile Devices (CCS 2022) used acoustic hand geometry for biometric authentication with strong liveness guarantees.

milestones.title: On the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters
milestones.note: Demonstrated that widely deployed password meters poorly predict real strength, misleading users about password quality.

milestones.title: Yet Another Text Captcha Solver: A Generative Adversarial Network Based Approach
milestones.note: Used GANs with minimal training data to break many deployed text CAPTCHA schemes, motivating CAPTCHA redesign.

milestones.title: Domain Validation++ For MitM-Resilient PKI
milestones.note: Strengthened CA domain validation to resist network-level man-in-the-middle attacks at certificate issuance.

milestones.title: PatternListener: Cracking Android Pattern Lock Using Acoustic Signals
milestones.note: Recovered Android pattern lock gestures from microphone-captured acoustic reflections.

milestones.title: Protocols for Checking Compromised Credentials
milestones.note: Designed privacy-preserving credential breach checking so users avoid revealing their passwords to the checker.

milestones.title: DeMiCPU: Device Fingerprinting with Magnetic Signals Radiated by CPU
milestones.note: Fingerprinted devices using distinctive CPU magnetic-field emissions, enabling authentication without additional hardware.

milestones.title: The Cookie Hunter: Automated Black-box Auditing for Web Authentication and Authorization Flaws
milestones.note: Automatically discovered authentication and authorization bugs in web applications via black-box testing.

milestones.title: EchoHand: High Accuracy and Presentation Attack Resistant Hand Authentication on Commodity Mobile Devices
milestones.note: Provided high-accuracy hand authentication on commodity phones with acoustic signals and strong anti-spoofing.

ndss.narrative:
Authentication research at NDSS has evolved from classical password security into an increasingly rich study of biometric, behavioral, and hardware-rooted mechanisms—alongside their attacks. A Security Analysis of Honeywords (NDSS 2018) set the tone early by showing that widely-deployed decoy-password systems were weaker than claimed, while a cluster of biometric papers examined camera-based authentication, fingerprint API misuse, and behavioral signals.

The 2019–2021 period introduced novel authenticators exploiting unconventional sensing. OcuLock (NDSS 2020) used electrooculography in VR headsets; rtCaptcha and Face Flashing proposed real-time liveness checks; SMS OTP insecurity was formally documented (On the Insecurity of SMS One-Time Password Messages, NDSS 2021); and FIDO UAF received its first systematic formal analysis. The theme was diversity: researchers demonstrated both that new modalities could work and that existing ones had exploitable gaps.

From 2022 onward physical-layer attacks became central. PHYjacking (NDSS 2022) hijacked hardware inputs to bypass authorization; PrintListener (NDSS 2024) inferred fingerprint patterns from friction sounds; EMIRIS (NDSS 2025) eavesdropped on iris biometrics via electromagnetic emanations. At the same time, anti-tracking cellular authentication (AAKA, NDSS 2024) and FIDO2 local-attack analysis signaled that the community is increasingly attentive to identity-linkage risks alongside pure spoofing threats.

milestones.title: A Security Analysis of Honeywords
milestones.note: Analyzes the security of honeyword decoy-password schemes, revealing weaknesses in detecting password-database breaches.

milestones.title: Robust Performance Metrics for Authentication Systems
milestones.note: Shows common authentication-system metrics are inadequate and proposes robust performance metrics for ML-based authentication.

milestones.title: OcuLock: Exploring Human Visual System for Authentication in Virtual Reality Head-mounted Display
milestones.note: OcuLock authenticates VR users by leveraging electrooculography signals of the human visual system in head-mounted displays.

milestones.title: On the Insecurity of SMS One-Time Password Messages against Local Attackers in Modern Mobile Devices
milestones.note: Shows local attackers on modern mobile devices can intercept SMS one-time passwords, undermining their security.

milestones.title: PHYjacking: Physical Input Hijacking for Zero-Permission Authorization Attacks on Android
milestones.note: Hijacks physical hardware inputs on Android to perform zero-permission authorization attacks like fingerprint and payment confirmation.

milestones.title: SoundLock: A Novel User Authentication Scheme for VR Devices Using Auditory-Pupillary Response
milestones.note: Authenticates VR users via auditory-pupillary response as a biometric.

milestones.title: AAKA: An Anti-Tracking Cellular Authentication Scheme Leveraging Anonymous Credentials
milestones.note: Proposes an anti-tracking cellular authentication scheme using anonymous credentials to prevent operators from tracking subscriber locations.

milestones.title: EMIRIS: Eavesdropping on Iris Information via Electromagnetic Side Channel
milestones.note: Eavesdrops on iris biometric data via electromagnetic side channels from recognition devices.

sp.narrative:
Authentication research at IEEE S&P covers password security, hardware tokens, biometrics, and voice-based identity. The 2018 cohort set foundational empirical baselines. On the Economics of Offline Password Cracking (S&P 2018) modeled adversary cost curves for dictionary attacks, providing a principled framework for setting password policy. A Tale of Two Studies: The Best and Worst of YubiKey Usability (S&P 2018) documented how deployment context, not hardware, determines security-token success.

The 2019-2020 period shifted toward neural models and emerging standards. Beyond Credential Stuffing: Password Similarity Models Using Neural Networks (S&P 2019) showed that neural models can predict password variants far better than rule-based guessing, raising the bar for breach-reuse attacks. Dangerous Skills (S&P 2019) highlighted authentication weaknesses in voice-assistant ecosystems. Is FIDO2 the Kingslayer of User Authentication? (S&P 2020) provided a usability verdict on passwordless authentication at scale, and Fidelius: Protecting User Secrets from Compromised Browsers (S&P 2019) built hardware-assisted protection for browser-submitted credentials.

From 2021, authentication papers diversified to decentralized identity and speaker recognition attack. Who is Real Bob? Adversarial Attacks on Speaker Recognition Systems (S&P 2021) demonstrated spoofing of voice-based authentication with synthesized speech. CanDID: Can-Do Decentralized Identity with Legacy Compatibility (S&P 2021) designed a Sybil-resistant decentralized identity system compatible with existing PKI. Improving Password Guessing via Representation Learning (S&P 2021) used neural embeddings to improve cracking.

By 2022-2024, the track expanded to AR/VR authentication (SoK: Authentication in Augmented and Virtual Reality, S&P 2022) and zero-knowledge credential systems (zk-creds, S&P 2023), reflecting the constant need to re-examine authentication assumptions as interaction modalities change.

uss.narrative:
The earliest papers here, all from USENIX 2018, treat passwords as a stubborn fact of life and try to understand or patch their weaknesses rather than replace them. Several are empirical and human-centered: "Better managed than memorized? Studying the Impact of Managers on Password Strength and Reuse" (2018) and "Forgetting of Passwords: Ecological Theory and Data" (2018) probe how real users cope with memory and tooling, while "The Rewards and Costs of Stronger Passwords in a University" (2018) studies how an actual password policy plays out at scale. Alongside these sit early systems and protocol concerns — "Rethinking Access Control and Authentication for the Home Internet of Things (IoT)" (2018) reframes authentication for multi-user device settings, and "O Single Sign-Off, Where Art Thou?" (2018) exposes session and account-hijacking gaps in SSO. This year sets the tone: passwords are insecure but entrenched, so the work is about measuring damage and hardening the ecosystem.

By 2019-2020 the field pivots from individual passwords toward the broader account-protection ecosystem and toward biometrics as an alternative. "Protecting accounts from credential stuffing with password breach alerting" (USENIX 2019) operationalizes breach data to defend accounts at scale, and "Birthday, Name and Bifacial-security" (2019) broadens the empirical lens beyond English-speaking users to Chinese passwords. At the same time, biometrics and liveness become central: "Void: A fast and light voice liveness detection system" (USENIX 2020) and "Liveness is Not Enough: Enhancing Fingerprint Authentication with Behavioral Biometrics to Defeat Puppet Attacks" (2020) show both the promise and the spoofing risks of biometric factors. Two-factor authentication also arrives as a serious object of study with "Empirical Measurement of Systemic 2FA Usability" (2020), shifting attention from whether 2FA is secure to whether organizations can actually live with it.

From 2021 to 2022 the work increasingly targets adoption, deployment, and the fragility of newer factors. "Driving 2FA Adoption at Scale" (USENIX 2021) turns 2FA into a design and behavioral problem of nudging users, while "Inexpensive Brainwave Authentication" (2021) and "Card Brand Mixup Attack" (2021) explore exotic biometrics and break real payment-card authentication respectively. Deepfakes raise the stakes for biometric trust in "Seeing is Living? Rethinking the Security of Facial Liveness Verification in the Deepfake Era" (USENIX 2022), and email-authentication measurement matures with "A Large-scale and Longitudinal Measurement Study of DKIM Deployment" (2022).

Most recently, USENIX 2023 shows two clear fronts. On classic passwords, machine learning sharpens guessing attacks and evaluation — "Improving Real-world Password Guessing Attacks via Bi-directional Transformers" (2023), "Password Guessing Using Random Forest" (2023), and "Pass2Edit" (2023) model how users create and edit passwords, while "No Single Silver Bullet: Measuring the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters" (2023) audits the meters meant to guide users. On the ecosystem side, "A Study of Multi-Factor and Risk-Based Authentication Availability" (2023) measures how far real services have actually moved beyond plain passwords, and emerging interfaces draw scrutiny in "Hidden Reality: Caution, Your Hand Gesture Inputs in the Immersive Virtual World are Visible to All!" (2023). The arc runs from measuring password pain, to building account-protection and biometric defenses, to ML-driven attack/defense and broad measurement of whether multi-factor and risk-based authentication are reaching users.

top4.narrative:
The 2018 papers in this list show a field organized around two long-standing problems: making text passwords less brittle, and patching the systems built on top of them. On the password side, work focused on measuring and improving the basics, from auditing how well password strength meters actually predict resistance to cracking ("On the Accuracy of Password Strength Meters," CCS 2018) to modeling the economics of an offline cracker ("On the Economics of Offline Password Cracking," S&P 2018) and even using fake "honeyword" decoys to detect breaches ("A Security Analysis of Honeywords," NDSS 2018). A parallel thread treated authentication as a systems problem: single sign-on session hijacking ("O Single Sign-Off, Where Art Thou?," USENIX 2018), local IPC attacks on security keys ("Man-in-the-Machine," USENIX 2018), and the human-factors reality that two-factor hardware is hard to use ("A Tale of Two Studies: The Best and Worst of YubiKey Usability," S&P 2018). Early biometric and side-channel work also appeared, from liveness detection ("Face Flashing," NDSS 2018) to inferring Android unlock patterns from sound ("PatternListener," CCS 2018).

The big shift in 2019 was the rise of credential reuse and breach-driven attacks as a first-class research target. Once billions of leaked passwords were public, the question became how to defend at scale, and a tight cluster of papers answered it: Google's breach-alerting deployment ("Protecting accounts from credential stuffing with password breach alerting," USENIX 2019), neural models that predict how attackers tweak a leaked password for a different site ("Beyond Credential Stuffing: Password Similarity Models Using Neural Networks," S&P 2019), and the cryptographic protocols ("Protocols for Checking Compromised Credentials," CCS 2019) needed to check leaks without leaking. The same period broadened the lens beyond English speakers ("Birthday, Name and Bifacial-security," USENIX 2019) and pushed machine learning deeper into guessing, culminating in representation-learning attacks ("Improving Password Guessing via Representation Learning," S&P 2021).

Around 2020 the field began seriously imagining a world after passwords, while also confronting new sensors and form factors. "Is FIDO2 the Kingslayer of User Authentication?" (S&P 2020) put passwordless FIDO2/WebAuthn under a usability microscope, signaling that standards-based public-key authentication was finally deployable. At the same time, biometrics matured from a feature into an arms race: voice liveness detection ("Void," USENIX 2020), behavioral defenses against fingerprint puppet attacks ("Liveness is Not Enough," USENIX 2020), and adversarial attacks that fool speaker recognition outright ("Who is Real Bob?," S&P 2021). Empirical studies grounded mobile reality, quantifying how guessable smartphone PINs are ("This PIN Can Be Easily Guessed," S&P 2020) and giving deployable password-policy advice ("Practical Recommendations for Stronger, More Usable Passwords," CCS 2020).

Most recently the frontier has moved in two directions. First, authentication for emerging platforms, with AR/VR becoming its own subarea ("OcuLock," NDSS 2020; "SoK: Authentication in Augmented and Virtual Reality," S&P 2022) and privacy-preserving biometrics on commodity hardware ("EchoHand," CCS 2022). Second, a cryptographic reimagining of identity itself, moving from "do I know your password" toward provable, privacy-preserving credentials: decentralized, Sybil-resistant identity ("CanDID," S&P 2021) and anonymous credentials built on zkSNARKs atop existing identity infrastructure ("zk-creds," S&P 2023). The throughline across these venues is a steady migration away from shared secrets toward cryptographic keys, liveness-aware biometrics, and verifiable-yet-private identity.
